gaps.sentence: My colleague Anna, ___ joined us in May, has already been promoted.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' refers to Anna; non-defining clauses never use 'that'.

gaps.sentence: The moment ___ she saw the results, she burst into tears.
gaps.explanation: 'When' links the moment to the action; 'where' and 'why' do not fit a time noun.

gaps.sentence: There are cases ___ this rule simply does not apply.
gaps.explanation: 'Cases where ...' means 'cases in which ...'; 'that' cannot introduce the clause without a subject.

gaps.sentence: Show me ___ you have written so far.
gaps.explanation: 'What you have written' means 'the things that you have written'; 'that' cannot head a nominal clause after 'me'.

gaps.sentence: The house ___ stands on the corner dates from 1870.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' is needed because a house is a thing; 'where' would introduce information about location, not a subject.

gaps.sentence: The programme ___ I watched last night was about volcanoes.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' refers to things, even when it is the object of the clause.

gaps.sentence: It was the first time ___ I had ever driven on my own.
gaps.hint: after 'the first time', use this pronoun
gaps.explanation: 'The first time that ...' is the standard pattern; the pronoun may also be omitted, but 'which' and 'what' do not fit.

gaps.sentence: He showed me the drawer in ___ the keys were kept.
gaps.explanation: 'In which' is the formal relative pattern for things; 'in where' is ungrammatical.
